justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I inferred was a current price near 357–358, likely for an asset such as an equity index, commodity, or similar instrument. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed level, adjusting slightly upward to reflect typical positive drift in risk assets and mean-reversion tendencies over very short windows. At one week, I extended that drift modestly, assuming no major catalysts would dramatically reprice the asset but acknowledging that small directional momentum could accumulate. At one month, the point estimate rises a bit further, consistent with a long-run positive expected return assumption, though the incremental gain is deliberately modest since mean-reversion and volatility tend to dominate over noise at that horizon.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect increasing uncertainty as the time horizon extends. At one day, realized volatility is relatively constrained — most assets don't move more than 1–3% in a single session absent a shock — so I kept the range tight at roughly plus or minus 9–10 points. Over one week, intraday and day-to-day volatility compounds, and the possibility of a macro announcement, earnings release, or geopolitical event widens the plausible range considerably. At one month, the interval nearly triples in half-width compared to one day, capturing the realistic possibility of a trending move, a sharp correction, or a sustained rally driven by factors not visible at the time of forecasting.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode — triggered by a central bank surprise, a financial stability concern, or an unexpected geopolitical escalation — could easily push the one-month outcome below 320. Liquidity shocks or a sharp repricing in correlated markets (such as bonds or currencies) could amplify moves beyond normal volatility regimes. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-covering rally could push the asset well above 410.

Finally, my intervals assume roughly stationary volatility and no structural breaks in the data-generating process. In practice, volatility clusters, and if the asset enters a high-volatility regime shortly after the forecast is made, even the one-day interval could prove too narrow. Model error — meaning my uncertainty about what the underlying asset even is and what its recent volatility has been — also implicitly widens the true uncertainty beyond what my stated intervals suggest. Readers should treat these intervals as informed approximations rather than precise probabilistic commitments.
